newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - Takeover wave to roll on in oil industry.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Takeover wave to roll on in oil industry.

text.p: A wave of takeovers, mergers and co-operation pacts in the oil industry is set to roll on in 1997 after several mega-alliances rocked the sector earlier this year.

In the upstream business the big players have ample cash to gobble up smaller firms, while poor refining and fuels markets will remain an impetus for tie-ups among equals in the downstream operations, analysts said.

But after Mobil Corp and British Petroleum Co Plc agreed to merge their European downstream operations and Shell and Texaco Inc announced they might do the same in the U.S., analysts believe there is not much scope left for deals of a similar size in refining and marketing.
But they rule nothing out, saying the remaining major companies -- such as Amoco Corp, Chevron Corp and Exxon Corp -- may feel drastic action is needed.
"Now we've got four of them, there may be two others to do it," said Richard Wilson, partner at Ernst & Young Energy Services.
But he reckons there is only a chance of about 20 percent this will actually happen.

Industry watchers rather believe any reshufflings will be along the lines of the deal struck between Shell and Mobil in November, whereby both giants agreed to merge their Californian exploration and production business.
Like this one, new deals among the big players will likely focus on a relatively small geographical areas and will be limited to specific business segments.
EUROPE AND U.S. TO REMAIN CENTRE OF ACTIVITY
Europe and the U.S. will likely remain the centres of such corporate activity. Being one of the most competitive fuels markets, Britain especially will see more tie-ups, experts said.
Asia, however, will likely be spared most of the downstream consolidation: it is a long-term growth market, even though this region too is currently suffering from too much refining capacity.
"If you oversupply the market in Asia you know that demand will catch up again, but if you oversupply Europe or North America you know you're stuck with it," said analyst Nick Antill at broker BZW.

In sharp contrast to the defensive mood in the downstream sector, the picture in upstream looks far more aggressive. Here is where money can still be made and where cash-rich oil majors have shown a strong appetite for outright takeovers.
"We are going to see a lot more asset acquisitions in the exploration and production area because after years of cost cutting the major oil companies are extremely cash flow positive," said Antill.
One of the companies frequently rumoured to be on the verge of an acquisition is Royal Dutch/Shell Group, the oil giant which sits on a cash pile of about eight billion pounds ($13 billion).
The Anglo-Dutch concern was last said to be eyeing British exploration and production firm LASMO Plc after earlier denying market talk it was interested in buying British Gas Plc.

The latest actual acquisition in the upstream sector took place two weeks ago when Norway's Saga Petroleum ASA paid $1.23 billion for Santa Fe Exploration, active in the British part of the North Sea, from Kuwait Petroleum Corporation.
Gulf Canada Resources on Wednesday launched a 432 million pound bid for Britain's Clyde Petroleum Plc.
LOWER OIL PRICE WILL NOT DETER COMPANIES
The widely-held expectation that oil prices will retreat in the course of next year, will not deter big companies from making acquisitions, analysts said.

They see see oil prices falling back to about $18-1/2 pre barrel during 1997 after after a surpisingly high average of around $20 per barrel so far in 1996. At the beginning of the year experts had predicted levels of $17.
But a host of factors, such as cold winter weather, lower than expected non-Opec production, low heating oil inventories and the absence of Iraq on world markets, wrongfooted analysts.
Chances of the same extraordinary combination lasting into the new year are small, industry watchers say.
One thing has already changed: Iraq recently agreed a food-for-oil deal with the United Nations and started exports last weekend.

The forecast retreat of oil prices will not help making life any easier for oil majors. Though closures of several refineries, may offer some relief in the downstream business, corporate earnings in 1997 are seen stable at best, experts said.
"On balance it is probably going to be a somewhat tougher year than it was in 1996," said Gordon Gray at Salomon Brothers.
Where does this leave shares?

Many analysts describe the outlook for integrated companies -- active in both the downstream and upstream sectors -- as basically trendless, but many see good increases for shares in exploration and production firms.
"The exploration companies will continue to be pushed by a combination of exploration success and corporate activity," said Antill.
